messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 68
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: European
- Relationship Status: Married
- Occupation: Psychologist
- Trauma Type: Physical abuse by romantic partner
- Pcl5: 61

He is 68 now, married, and for most of his adult life he has been the one other people come to when they are frightened, ashamed, or trying to make sense of pain. He works as a psychologist, a role that suits the careful way he listens and the way he tends to think before speaking. But when he talks about what happened in his own life, his voice changes. He becomes quieter, more deliberate, as if he is moving around broken glass.

The violence began in a relationship he once describes as “intense from the start.” At first, he remembers the partner’s attention as flattering, almost intoxicating. The jealousy that later turned into control arrived gradually, disguised as devotion. There were comments about who he saw, what he wore, how long he stayed at work. He tells himself for a long time that it was only conflict, only personality, only stress. He is someone trained to observe patterns in others, yet in his own life he keeps revising the story to make it less alarming. That habit delays his recognition of danger.

The first shove is dismissed. The first slap is followed by apologies, tears, promises, and a period of tenderness so convincing that he feels foolish for being frightened. Over time, the abuse becomes more direct and more humiliating. He is grabbed by the arms, thrown against walls, pinned in doorways, struck hard enough to leave bruises that he covers with long sleeves and invented explanations. He begins to track the sound of footsteps in the house, the tone of a voice, the way a door is closed, because his body learns before his mind does. He lives in a state of braced expectation, always preparing for the next eruption.

When the relationship finally ends, it is not because he feels ready. It ends because the fear becomes impossible to negotiate. Even then, the violence does not fully leave him. He continues to feel watched, as if anger might still be waiting just outside the room. For a long time afterward, he startles at sudden noise and flinches when someone approaches from behind. He avoids conflict of any kind, including ordinary disagreement with colleagues or family members, because raised voices bring back the same tightness in his chest and the old certainty that something bad is about to happen. He keeps himself busy, overfunctions at work, and maintains a polished composure that few people would suspect is built on vigilance.

In his practice, he remains competent and thoughtful, but he notices how often certain stories in his patients pull him off balance. He can stay calm when he is listening to others, yet later find himself unsettled by a simple phrase or a description of coercion. He becomes more careful about seating positions in rooms and prefers to have his back to a wall. At night he scans the house before settling, checking locks more than once. Sleep is light and broken. He wakes with a racing heart after dreams he does not always remember, only a residue of dread and the sense that he has been fighting in his sleep.

There are triggers he dislikes admitting. A hand raised in an animated conversation can make him freeze. The smell of alcohol on someone’s breath can tighten his stomach. He avoids certain places that remind him of the period when he felt trapped and small. He also avoids talking about the abuse in any depth, even with his wife, who knows enough to understand that he has been altered by something she could not fully witness. He is affectionate with her and clearly devoted, yet there are moments when he goes distant without warning, especially if he feels cornered emotionally. In those moments he retreats into silence, not because he does not care, but because some part of him still believes that speaking openly invites danger.

What is most striking is how long he has continued to carry both the knowledge and the shame. He says he should have left earlier. He says he should have seen it sooner. He speaks about himself with a severity he rarely uses with anyone else. And yet, beneath that self-criticism, there is also grief: grief for the years lost to fear, grief for the version of himself that had to stay alert in his own home, grief that the person he trusted became the source of threat. Even now, after all this time, he lives with a body that remembers what his mind would prefer to keep at a distance.
